lead.eyebrow: ⚡ Wednesday Open — Hormuz Flows Recover, but Iranian Tanker Attacks Keep Brent Pinned Near $100
lead.headline: Brent Edges Up to $101.35 as Gulf Exports Top Pre-War Levels — Yet Iran Escalates Tanker Attacks and Stockpiles Remain "Scarily Thin"
paragraphs: Brent crude rose 0.77% to $101.35 a barrel on Wednesday, according to Trading Economics, extending a market that has spent the week oscillating around the $100 handle. The move came after Brent briefly slipped below $100 on Tuesday, when oil futures fell about 2.5% on news that the G7 would release 100 million barrels from emergency reserves and that Hormuz volumes were normalising. Trading Economics attributed the latest bid to Iran's intensified attacks on tankers, with the UK Maritime Trade Operations reporting nine incidents so far in October. Brent remains roughly 38% above its pre-war level near $73, so the geopolitical premium is still large. Trading Economics quotes differ slightly by provider and contract, so treat the print as indicative rather than a settlement.

The supply picture has improved materially. OilPrice.com, citing Reuters and Kpler data, reported that Hormuz flows reached pre-war levels at 19.5–22.5 million barrels a day over September 27–29, roughly double the level a month earlier, while CBS News said Middle East exports topped pre-war levels at about 19.2 million bpd last week. Shell CEO Wael Sawan put flows at "80-plus percent" of pre-war, a reminder that estimates differ by methodology and by whether Iranian barrels are counted, and the divergence matters for how much more supply the market can still absorb. Trading Economics added that Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline has been restored to 5.8 million bpd, a key bypass if Hormuz or Red Sea routes are disrupted. The gap between these estimates is itself a source of volatility.

The bullish counterweight is inventories and security. Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser warned that global stockpiles are "scarily thin" and that replenishing them while meeting demand could take up to two years, with nearly 3 billion barrels of supply lost since the war began on February 28. Houthi strikes on Saudi targets and a Saudi-led coalition counteroffensive in Yemen keep the Red Sea in play, and UK diesel at a record 199.52 pence a litre shows the product market remains far tighter than crude. The result: crude is capped by returning barrels and G7 stock releases, but dips are being bought because the buffer is so thin, and any new disruption would land on a market with little room to absorb it, which is why traders are not yet willing to push Brent decisively below $100.

news.headline: Brent Climbs to $101.35 as Iranian Tanker Attacks Offset Improving Supply
news.body: Trading Economics put Brent at $101.35, up 0.77%, on Wednesday, saying prices rose as Middle East tensions persisted. It cited UKMTO data showing nine attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz so far this month, while noting upward pressure was limited by better supply: Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline has been restored to 5.8 million barrels a day, and industry data showed US crude inventories falling 2.1 million barrels the previous week. The takeaway for traders is a market boxed in between returning barrels and persistent shipping risk, with the war premium of roughly $28 over the pre-war price of about $73 proving sticky. For diesel, any shipping disruption feeds directly into freight and insurance costs.

news.headline: Oil Falls as Kpler Says Hormuz Crude Flows Topped Pre-War Levels
news.body: OilPrice.com reported on October 5 that Brent traded near $101.20 and WTI at $89.73 after Reuters cited provisional Kpler data showing Hormuz flows of 19.5–22.5 million barrels a day on September 27–29, around double the volume a month earlier. LNG exports reportedly returned to pre-war volumes as well, though QatarEnergy remains under force majeure. Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and Iranian tanker incidents continued regardless. The data suggests physical crude supply is no longer the binding constraint, shifting the focus to refined products and security. It also strengthens the bearish case that Brent could drift toward the mid-$90s if the flow recovery holds without a major incident.

news.headline: ICE Low Sulphur Gasoil Slides to $1,384.25/mt, Down 3.87% on the Day
news.body: TradingView showed ICE Low Sulphur Gasoil (ULS1!, October 2026 contract) at $1,384.25 per tonne, down 3.87% over 24 hours, with the market closed at the time of the print. The contract is still down 8.39% over five days and 5.17% over one month, yet up 115.65% year to date and 98.14% on the year. Investing.com recorded a sharp rally on October 2 on re-escalating tanker attacks across Hormuz and the Gulf of Aden. The pattern is a volatile, headline-driven market where gasoil spikes on attacks and retreats on flow data. With UK retail diesel at a record, the physical squeeze has not eased, so dips look fragile.

news.headline: G7 Pledges 100 Million Barrels From Emergency Reserves as WTI Slips Below $90
news.body: Fox News reported that WTI fell below $90 to $89.61 and Brent eased to $101.82 after G7 nations pledged to release 100 million barrels from emergency stockpiles. CBS News added that consuming nations plan releases to curb price pressure, and Investing.com said President Trump is exploring measures to lower domestic fuel costs ahead of the midterm elections. A 100-million-barrel release is equivalent to about a day of global demand, so it is a bridge and a psychological cap more than a structural fix. It does, however, reduce the chance of an upside spike unless physical flows are hit, and it deepens the need to refill reserves later, which would be supportive for prices next year.

news.headline: Houthis Target Riyadh Airport and Rabigh Refinery as Saudi-Led Coalition Strikes Yemen
news.body: Fox News reported that the Iran-backed Houthis claimed strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco refinery in Rabigh, Abha airport and the Khamis Mushait base on October 5. Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said Operation "Dawn of Yemen" used 100 fighter jets to destroy 324 targets, including weapons depots and naval mines in Hodeidah province. Yemen's government claims full control of Bab al-Mandeb and Perim Island. Such claims remain unverified, but the Red Sea is the main alternative route to Hormuz. Any confirmed damage to Rabigh or Red Sea loading would hit the bypass logic that has kept Saudi exports flowing, and would hit product markets hardest.

news.headline: Aramco's Nasser: Global Stockpiles "Scarily Thin"; Refill Could Take Two Years
news.body: CBS News live coverage quoted Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser warning that global stockpiles are "scarily thin," while Fox News reported his estimate that replenishing inventories while meeting demand could take up to two years, with nearly 3 billion barrels of supply lost since the conflict started. Shell CEO Wael Sawan said Middle East flows were at 80-plus percent of pre-war levels, and UK diesel hit a record 199.52 pence per litre. The message from the industry is that flow normalisation does not equal market normalisation: low stocks amplify any disruption and keep backwardation and product cracks elevated, which supports both Brent and especially diesel even as headline crude eases.

events.name: EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report
events.impact: The latest EIA figures I could verify (week ended September 25) showed crude up 922,000 barrels to 427.3 million and distillates down 2.3 million, 14% below average. Trading Economics cited industry data pointing to a 2.1 million-barrel crude draw in the latest week. Today's print will show whether distillates keep falling despite higher refinery runs. A further diesel draw would reinforce gasoil's premium; a build would support the recent softness.

events.name: Hormuz Tanker Attacks and Iranian Conditions
events.impact: UKMTO counts nine incidents in October already, and Iran's IRGC has ordered vessels to turn back or face targeting. Tehran also says Hormuz stays shut until US demands are met. A tanker loss or an attack that cuts Kpler-tracked flows would restore the war premium quickly and lift freight and insurance costs; a quiet week would let Brent test the mid-$90s as volumes normalise.

events.name: Houthi / Saudi Red Sea Escalation
events.impact: The Saudi-led coalition's Operation Dawn of Yemen and Houthi claims on Rabigh and Riyadh put the Red Sea bypass at risk. Verified damage to Aramco refining or loading infrastructure would hit product supply hardest, because Gulf refineries are already running below normal. Absent confirmation, the market continues to price this as an option rather than lost barrels.

events.name: G7 Emergency Stock Release Implementation
events.impact: The 100-million-barrel pledge needs a delivery schedule. Details on timing, volumes per country and whether the US participates will determine how much it caps prompt prices. A slow or small release would disappoint a market that cites 'scarily thin' stocks, while a front-loaded schedule would pressure the prompt spreads and Brent toward the mid-$90s.

events.name: OPEC+ Monthly Review and Spare Capacity
events.impact: OPEC+ left quotas unchanged for November according to prior reporting, and the group continues monthly reviews. With stocks depleted and Gulf output still recovering, spare capacity is thin, so the group's ability to cushion a fresh disruption is limited. Watch for signals on December quotas and any Saudi pricing moves, such as the recent cut to Asia's Arab Light price.
events.market_impact: Low near term; shapes the Q4 floor.

paragraphs: Yesterday I argued that Brent was a range trade, with Hormuz diplomacy as the swing factor. Today's tape confirms it: Brent is at $101.35, up 0.77%, after dipping below $100 on Tuesday. The market is balancing record-high Gulf flows against a steady drumbeat of tanker attacks, and neither side has yet won, and the range has held for several sessions. Nine incidents in the first week of October is not a trivial number, and the reaction so far has been muted because the barrels are still arriving. That can change quickly if an attack removes a cargo or forces insurers to reprice transit risk, so the calm deserves some scepticism.

My read on today: The crude side of the equation is healing, and the data keep saying so: Kpler flows at pre-war levels, Middle East exports near 19.2 million bpd, Saudi's East-West line at 5.8 million bpd. Add the G7 pledge of 100 million barrels and the case for much higher crude weakens. I would not chase a rally above $104 without verified damage to infrastructure, because the stock release and recovering flows create a cap. The natural gas tape, up to $3.13 on lower output and firmer LNG feedgas, is a side show for crude today.

Diesel is the other story. ICE Low Sulphur Gasoil at $1,384.25 per tonne is down 3.87% on the day but still more than double its level of a year ago, and UK retail diesel is at a record. Refinery damage and thin inventories mean product tightness lags crude's recovery, so the diesel crack is likely to stay elevated even if Brent drifts lower. Sharp gasoil drops have repeatedly been followed by rebounds on fresh attacks. Watch the gasoil curve structure as well: a persistently steep backwardation would signal that buyers still fear prompt shortages despite the recovery in crude flows.

The bigger picture: This is a low-inventory market priced as if supply were normal. That asymmetry argues for respecting upside tail risk even in a flat tape. My call: Brent trades $97–$104 today, flat with an upward skew if tanker attacks hit flow data. A credible Hormuz reopening timetable is the only catalyst for a sustained break below $95. Traders should also keep in mind that the week's EIA print and any G7 delivery schedule can move prompt spreads before they move flat price.
